Here is the long awaited tournament report for Blood Siege - The
Western Canadian Qualifier for the North American Championship - that
was held in St. Albert, Alberta, Canada, on Aug. 25. Enjoy.

The story so far . . .

Dawn's first light streamed with the river beneath the Low Level
Bridge in Edmonton. Wedged precariously among the beams above the
water, Jennie Orne said a quiet prayer. Night had surrendered its hold
over the city to the day again, and none to soon for her cramped arms
and legs. Signs of the monster, the one who called himself 'Vignes',
had vanished along with it, but he would be back. If she knew anything
about the monster that had stalked her amidst the violence of the
fading night, it was this: he would not relinquish the power that he
had held over the City of Champions so easily. This time the Champions
had caught him off guard, in no small part due to the distraction from
the south. Routing Vignes and his kind would not be so easy next time.

Nostoket allowed himself a slight smile as news from the battlefield
filtered in. Preliminary reports suggested the Tzimisce's ghouls had
caught the Brujah and their pathetic Nosferatu spies napping in their
crypts during the initial assault. And the Ahrimanes had done an
admirable job of blocking the escape routes and mopping up pockets of
resistance in their wake. It was only a matter of time before the
Sword wrested control of the city away from the cowardly Ventrue. It
may very well have succeeded this time, if not for the mortals . . . .

Nostoket smiled again. No doubt howls of anger and disbelief would
erupt from the Camarilla once news of the mortals' stake in the city
spread. No matter: the Sabbat could fight two enemies as easily as it
could one. More concerning were disturbing rumors about the re-
emergence of the "Lords of the Night." The Sword of Caine would need
to tread cautiously . . .

The rumors are true . . .

Twenty-one Methuselah's from Edmonton and Red Deer gathered at
Thunderground Comics on Aug. 25 for Blood Siege 2007. In addition to
battling for one of six spots at the North American Championships
later this month, the players vied for a chance to have their names
engraved for posterity on the Blood Siege trophy, featuring the
original artwork for the Sabbat War card of the same name.

I'd like to thank Roy Kim of Thunderground for doing such a great job
(as always) as host; Oscar Garza, for supplying shirts and promos
between moving offices and leaving for Gen Con; Jason Switner, Prince
of Edmonton, for all his help organizing the tournament and providing
additional prize support; and William O'Connor, for hunting through
his warehouse for the original art for Blood Siege.

Photographs of the trophy, which wil be displayed at Thunderground, as
well as the event are available, if anyone is interested in seeing
them.

I would also like to take a moment to say how proud I am of the four
players from Red Deer who attended this year's qualifier. A year ago,
there was only one person from Red Deer who made the trip up to
Edmonton (that would be me). Now there are eight Methuselah's who
regularly play VTES in Red Deer on Thursday nights, and three of them
qualified for the NAC. I'm hopeful Red Deer will continue to build on
its success. Way to go, boys and girls!

On to the tournament, which featured a wide variety of decks based on
the Camarilla, Sabbat, Independents, Laibon and Bloodlines. However,
five decks clearly dominated the field heading into the final:

Bob Eckert (War Ghouls - 2 GW 7 VPs) bleeding
Shawn Zinyk (Massasi Rush - 1 GW 4 VPs) bleeding
Michael Holmbert (Imbued - 2 GW 8 VPs) bleeding
Thomas Solway (Ventrue Dom Bleed - 2 GW 9 VPs) bleeding
Nick Fraser (Ahrimane Wall - 2 GW 7 VPs)

The final was over almost before it started. Despite building a nearly
impenetrable wall during the first two rounds, Nick jammed on combat
in the final. Thomas seized the initiative, ousting Nick and Bob.
Unfortunately for him, Massassi's rush limitation allowed Michael to
tool up the imbued virtually unimpeded. Once the imbued were set up,
it was only a matter of time before Michael ousted Thomas and Shawn
for the game win and the tournament victory

I completly disagree that the problem is the imbued. MoM is indeed
too powerful, but this deck packed 2 of them, no Parthenon and only 7
masters to use with Anthelios (which was probably used more as a
gateway event for EE). Players just don't understand Imbued. They
freak when they hit the table. I used to be one of those players, it
was all too much, so I went out and bought them because we only had 1
imbued player in my playgroup. After using them, I had a much greater
understanding of their strenghts and weaknesses and what cards did
what and how they interacted with the game mechanics. Until I owned
and played them I didn't get this - I was intimidated as a player when
they hit the table.

There are still a lot of players who just don't get it. This deck
isn't that scary. So what, it's got champions and loads of
disciplines. It's only got 3 .44's and no other maneuvers. They can
be hurt, even by light combat. And I mean really hurt. They don't
have any stealth other than Second Sight, which only gives them
effectively 2 stealth on any of their actions. They can be thefted,
crowed, or just bashed. If they've got 1 Champion, then you send 2
guys. They can't handle vote, they don't have much pool gain outside
of Travis (and even then - he gets blocked).

The players might not have the perfect deck for dealing with them, but
there are basic strategies that work against them. People just don't
want to or don't know how to deal with them.

Imbued in my playgroup don't win very often. Sure they might get a
couple VP, but when they do win it's rare. And that's because we can
deal with them. If everyone is playing Big Cap stealth bleed and can
only get 1 or 2 guys out and then get shut down - well that's a bad
deck design that they've made. It could get shut down by Deflection.

So yes, the problem lies with the Players on the table, not the
imbued.

> - get out of "torpor" without an action

Can be burnt in torpor with little fear of recrimination (ie no blood

> - get permanent intercept easily (Unmasking)

I'd hate to say that this isn't that easy.. how many unmasking will
you play in a deck.
Anyway, Gehenna (and events in general) have been around for a while
now, and there are a lot of very annoying ones, not just Unmasking.
They can be destroyed with Black Hand Ritual, Not to Be, Emergency
Preparations, and now Uncoiling.
And then, lets not forget about Break the Code. I stick one in plenty
of decks.... it doesn't hurt card flow, but can be very useful. If
you aren't building decks that are taking Gehenna into account than
that's your problem - not mine.

> - recycle the important stuff (Conviction)

So? If they couldn't recycle the convictions they'd be dead.

> - untap after putting powers in play

This is the only real gripe I have with their mechanics, and I'll
agree with you on this. They should be limited to 1 power a turn
(like Political Actions), or 1 untap per turn after getting a Power.

> - are not affected by cards like Decapitate and similar

That is a problem with the cards, not with the Imbued.

> - are weenies

I'd hesitate to say that they aren't really weenies. For mine,
weenies are 1-3 caps. 4-6 (which most Imbued are), is getting into
the realms of midcaps.

> - can equip via a Master OOT

And then they dont' get a master phase, or get to use Angel to untap.

> - have wake-potential

So do vampires, your point? This is really clutching at straws.
Their wake is either an OOT Master (yey), or a card that they can only
use once per minion between untaps, and then they don't untap as per
normal. That is hardly something to write home about.

Vampires have access to:
Special Report
Second Tradition
Guard Dogs
Rats Warning
Black Sunrise
Wake with Evening's Freshness
Forced Awakening
Read the Winds
Forced Vigiliance
On the Qui Vive (the only one that Allies can use)

and those are just the ones off the top of my head.

> - can stop any action (Champion)

Can stop a D action, and then still get bashed. It costs 2
conviction, of which they only get 1 back in their untap. Logistics
says they will run out. And if you actually try to run them out, you
will. Too many people stop trying to act against them once a Champion
hits the table... wtf? How dumb are people?

> - can cancel any action card (Determine)

Taken by their predator, which taps the minion stopping them using
that Reaction again, unless they wake with the OOT master or On the
Qui Vive which they can only use once and not untap. And Determine
costs them a conviction.

> - have acces to bounce

And? They don't get to direct where it goes. It again, costs them a
conviction and taps them. They have very limited wake potential.

> - can seldom be stolen/burned with actions

They are completely and I mean completely hosed when Sebastion Goulet
is merged. Granted this is just 1 vampire, but it shuts them down. I
don't see many vampire decks that are shut down when 1 minion hits the
table. And lets look at it anyway, they have to burn the React with
Conviction. Try the action twice.
As to burning them, man what are you smoking.

* Blood to Water
* Liquefy the Mortal Coil
* Entombment
* Basilk's Touch
* Mercy for Seth

are all combat cards that burn them outright. Who cares about damage
prevention or MoM, none of these do. And yes, I have decks that pack
3 of these cards. Why, well it's because I'm adapting to the game
environment and not stagnating.

What can burn a vampire with an action? Not many unless you include
diablerie, which is the same action as pillowfacing, without as I
mentioned earlier, the harsh recriminations that a blood hunt entails.

> - can hose vampires without hurting themselves (Gehenna Events).

I can do likewise with a non-discipline deck, I've got one. I'm sure
everyone has tried one just for shits and giggles. but this again is
Event card related, not Imbued. And lets not forget Break the Code
which can destroy Imbued.

> I think that's pretty tough.

I think your arguments are pretty lame. You've listed nothing really

There are plenty of ways to "deal with" an imbued deck, depending upon
what you mean by "deal with". If your goal is to defend yourself
against the imbued, you do it the same way you do against vampires:
block, bounce, bloat, or backrush. Backrushing can be a fair bit more
difficult against imbued than against vampires, but it can still work
depending on your deck (it actually works *better* if your deck is not
dedicated combat but more of a toolboxy/multiact deck with Break the
Code to provide the rush actions and some Freak Drives to follow-up
with an immediate pillowface).

If your goal is to *oust* the imbued player, that's a bit trickier.
I'm loathe to share all my secrets because, well, holding them close
helps keep me from getting ousted. But of the strategies I've played
against, only combat seems to require major tweaking to the deck
itself (and it's the kind of tweaking that's overall probably not
worth it).

So I'll just say that the first key to ousting an imbued player is to
mind their untaps. They only get one real wake per turn (Angel of
Berlin), and that only if they don't play another out-of-turn master
like DI or Sudden. They can potentially save a Vigilance or two for
your turn as well, so keep an eye out for that. On the Qui Vive might
make an appearance, but only half of the last ten recorded Imbued
tournament wins used *any* OtQV in the deck. The key to my own success
as an imbued player is to always leave enough untapped minions to
(potentially) block every minion my predator controls (there are
exceptions, of course). So you need to be able either avoid their
blocks (stealth/block fails), hurt them in combat (and survive their
hitback) when they block (guns and/or jackets other are good here), or
take more actions than they expect you to (Majesty/Freak Drive).

The second key to ousting an imbued player is to stop assuming that
all imbued decks are the same. People rant and rave about Champion
this and Determine that, but not every minion can play those cards.
Keep an eye on what minions and which virtues your prey is playing
with, and learn what type of deck he's playing:
-OtQV is significantly more likely to appear alongside imbued with
Vision, because it enables them to play Determine more often, either
bouncing your bleeds or canceling your action cards.
-If a bunch of minions with Judgment come up, it's probably a Darby
Dance deck (or at least a Vigilance deck). This kind of multiaction
can be brutal. Using Not to Be or The Uncoiling to kill Edge Explosion
or NRA PAC could be pretty effective. Alternatively, target that
laptop for destruction/pillowfacing.
-If the deck is playing Defense, and you're relying on stealthy (D)
actions, do whatever it takes to stop that Champion, either by DIing
it, blocking it, beating the minion up in combat (yes, this means that
stealth bleed decks should probably start including a couple of guns -
Champion can't stop that equip action and you've got plenty of stealth
to get by the Unmasking and whatnot, so Concealed/disguised is not
necessary). Alternatively, if you're not relying on stealth-bleeds,
that Champion is probably useless against you; block the Rejuvenate
instead. Do keep in mind that using Champion doesn't tap the imbued,
so it can be used as an expensive way to generate extra blocks.
-If you see a bunch of guys with different virtues and a methuselah
proudly announcing their special text every time he influences a new
one into play, he could be playing a "powerless" Flash Grenade/Wooden
Stake deck. Warning: this deck may not actually be powerless. Champion
is a common include, as is Discern. However, there probably won't be
very many copies, so if you can block/DI the one or two that _are_ in
there, you'll only have to deal with Unmasking/Second Sight getting in
the way of your actions.
-Break the Code is a really strong, low-opportunity cost anti-imbued
card. The -1 intercept is universally painful, particularly if you can
play it before The Unmasking hits the table, but the universal
uncovering of imbued havens is also pretty useful.

Another thing to keep in mind is that the imbued are a lot easier to
manage when you keep up the pressure. Backing off for even a moment
can enable them to get a much better setup against you. In "normal"
games of VtES, being too agressive early can garner table hate and
open you up to your predator. The latter part is still true when
you're preying on the imbued, but (depending on circumstance) you
ought to be able to use all this to your advantage assuming you can
deflect the table hate to your imbued prey. Keep in mind that while
the imbued can bounce, Determine is only usable as bounce when your
predator is acting - they can't bounce a bounced bleed. Creating the
illusion of an opening to provoke your predator into bleeding you
heavily so you can bounce it into your prey can help you get past
their defenses.

Okay, that's enough spewing for now. Take the lessons or don't, your
metagame may vary, etc.

Yeah, see, that is the main trick, now isn't it. Light intercept and

ability to always do 4 damage. And ya know how often that deck is
going to win? Probably not that often.

will slow down the Imbued, sure. But at the same time, the Imbued are
virtually impossible to oust with combat--you can't Fame or Haven
them, you can't Taste them. Tension doesn't really help against them.
Frontal assault doesn't work so well against them. They get out of the
hospital really easily. They have built in hitback defense (i.e. thay
always can hit you for 2 just 'cause they showed up). You can
pillowface them (if you don't get blocked...) but then you take more
damage--which is bad if you are a weenie Rush deck, which are the most

totally foils combat and flows freely in Imbued decks (or at least
should). You can beat them up easily, sure, but they recover quickly
and foil agressive combat left and right. You can beat them up. But
ousting them at the same time is really difficult. Which is, ya know,
the trick.

nothing for granted. Yeah, in deck design it's helpful to think of the
imbued as always having +2 intercept (Unmasking + Second Sight), +1
hands, +1 bleed, and so forth, so that you can think "Can my deck
handle +1 intercept all the time and frequent +2?" "Can my deck handle
frequent hitback for 2?" "What happens if I get hit with a bunch of
Flash Grenades?" and either alter your deck or not depending your
analysis. This kind of thing doesn't just help against imbued either -
it helps against any deck that frequently generates moderate intercept
(Second Tradition? Raven Spies? Channel 10?), moderate hitback
(Weighted Walking Stick? .44 Magnum?), or moderate bleed (Computer
Hacking? Laptops and Bleed retainers? Most decks in existence?).

_right now_ and what they've indicated their particular deck is
capable of (check the ash heap).

this aspect. Everything turns into "but if you pack X, it'll be
countered by Y!" "If that happens, do Z." "Then they'll play Q and all

imbued are broken if you need all that to defend against them" all the
while ignoring the fact that the imbued decks can't fit Y, Q, P, R,
and S all into their decks either, nor guarantee that they'll be

There are a few major components of the game.

1. Acting
2. Blocking
3. Combat

Acting may or may not involve stealth.
Blocking may or may not involve intercept
Combat occurs when B meets A.

Not every deck is going to pack stealth or intercept granted - but
that is a choice that you make when you build the deck. They are
fundamental aspects of the game. If you choose to build a deck that
concentrates on one aspect to the detriment of others, than you must
be prepared for the risks that entails. I build these decks myself,
all the time. When I am boned, i shrug and say "should have played
the other deck". It happens, but you've got to take the good with the
bad.

If because you choose to limit your deck creation to the tigh rather
than the adaptable, you cannot blame deck mechanics.

Imbued, by their mechanics are by default adaptable, but they then can
struggle to be focused, which can be their downfall. They have to
take the good with the bad when it comes to this. Imbued can't be
effected by cards like Disarm, Decpatitate and Taste - which we all
agree they should. MoM is broken when used with Imbued, but this is a
problem with those cards not with the Imbued themselves. But
conversely, Imbued cannot play cards such as Delaying Tactics and
Disengage as these cost a blood, which Imbued as allies do not have to
spend. Their power card, Champion, cannot stop Political Actions, and
they have very few ways of gaining votes shy of Mamam Boumba, Rose
Foundation and Surprise Influence. They cannot go Anarch to stop
dying to Anarch Revolts, and they cannot remove Smiling Jack. There
are plenty of cards to steal them, and combat cards that can burn them
- far far more common than there are to steal or burn vampires.

So, whilst there are cards that they don't interact with which is a
bonus to them, there are some that they don't interact with which can
screw them royally.

Their are pros and cons to both sides of the argument. I advocate
intercept and combat both in light terms as ways to deal with Imbued.
Their are others, one of which is constant pressure. People have to
learn to adapt to the metagame as Witness has said. People have
learnt to adapt to other metagame shifts, but seem reluctant to try
and move with Imbued.

I now include more Sudden Reversal/Wash in block decks than I did in
the past. But this isn't just anti-imbued tech to stop MoM, it is
also useful as pseudo forward motion. Having limited go forward,
every blood doll or Minion Tap that i can stop my prey getting is a
faux-bleed that I've done, so I look for options that are going to be
useful against both Imbued and Vampire crypt decks.

I've found myself slotting more and more options for combat into decks
rather than the simple maneuvers/dodge and S:CE that seem prevalent in
many tournamnet decks.

As i said above, sometimes i go with the tight deck, and it can pay
off or it can't. At the EC day 2, it definately did not pay off for
me, when I went obf/PRE heavy stealth bleed, and had wall decks as a
prey in all 3 games. I was sitting there thinking, meh, could have
played the combat deck like I thought about doing and I'd be ripping
these fella's apart. But that was a decision I went with and it
didn't pay off. At other events, I've gone with the tight deck and it
has worked wonders.

Again, these are decisions that you make when you build and play a
deck.

When my mate pulls out his corrupt deck and I'm playing weenies, it
can be very annoying, but shit happens. I just have to turn around
and bash him, or hope that I can oust my prey before he steals all my
guys.

So in short, suck it up and stop blaming mechanics for poor planning
or bad luck.

Actually, I feel I've been taking pains to NOT say that. I'm saying
you don't HAVE to have anything in your deck. I'm saying you have a
choice, and that even if you choose not to have *specifically* anti-

imbued. (I know, radical concept, but it's totally true!)
I'm just trying to figure out why you can't just slot anti-SB, anti-
Vote, anti-Weenie, anti-etc tech into many of these complaints about
"Arrrg, now I have to slot in anti-imbued tech"....which we could just
as well rewrite as "Man, I wish I didn't have to keep slotting in
bounce for all those S&B decks." or "Votes suck, now I have to pack
all these DT's and PP's in my deck."

We choose every time we build a deck, what we can fit in and what we
can't. Our choices don't necessarily make our deck inviable. I have
a deck with no bounce! NONE! It has performed admirably in many
games. I made a choice to not try to stuff bounce in, that is a risk
I take. Do I run around saying "Oh, but I'm *forced* by those mean
old developers to put bounce in my deck, otherwise Malks/!Malks will
eat my face when I sleep"? No...because it's not true!

Was that clear this time? Choice, choice, decisions, cost/benefit,
choice! No arm twisting, no gun to the head. No "Must Have or Die."
I'm not saying the consequence of not having anti-ally tech is loss,
but maybe it is a harder game. You make that choice for yourself, not
the developers, not your opponent, not the metagame. You.

Can you grasp that some strategies that work against the imbued might
be just peachy keen versus vampires? Is this a hard concept? Do I
have to list, at length, strategies that don't magically suck versus
all vampire decks ever? Maybe I do.

Mean things that target JUST imbued:
Break the Code

Some mean things that allies hate:
Far mastery
Lure of the serpent
Sebastian Goulet
Entrancement

Some mean things that work against allies/imbued/vampires:
Wall Decks: Block all that crap, everybody hates it when you block
their crap, whether their minions have a pulse or not.
Arms of the Abyss + Entombment: Imbued get burned, vampires get sent
to torpor. Yay!
Follow the Bouncing Bleed: Imbued really have to bleed to oust and
vampires have other options, but bleed is still popular.
Stealthy Votes: KRC works on everyone. Reins of Power and Ancient
Influence, already strong, get a significant boost against the
imbued. Champion useless!
Animalism: Popular here in Atlanta. Pack Alpha! Raven Spies!
Crowbat! It seems to work.
Anarch Revolt: Can't go Anarch, Can't vote it away? Then just die.

This is not a comprehensive list. This is a set of examples of
strategies that are employed successfully against vampires that now
happen to put some hurt to the imbued. Some of these may not work
against every Imbued deck, just like they won't work against every
vampire deck. It is a short list because I don't have all my life to
sit an think of everything and list it. Go find your own, that's the
joy of the game.

Blinded with Science!
-D

If we're getting philosophical, I'll tell you what I feel about this.

First of all, let me say that I don't believe in the CCG system working in
eternity. Bannings, set rotations, nerfings, etc. are needed to keep a CCG
both fun and challenging. This is not happening in V:TES the last years.
What we're getting is new mechanics and new rules. Most of them with only
marginal impact on the game. Note: I'm not blaming the Rules Team, nor LSJ
for this. It's a choice they in the past and they're sticking to it.

Secondly, I feel that -in a hypothetical 'perfect' game - perfect defences
shouldn't exist. Providing of course that attacks aren't as strong to need
perfect defences. (fr.ex. If bleed decks weren't as powerfull as they are
now, deflection didn't need to exist in its current form.)

Thirdly, I believe that the fact that you are already playing with
randomised cards, randomised seating and imperfect information about other
decks, luck is already a big enough factor. Every way of dimishing the luck
factor is good, imo. (fr.ex some way of keeping people from being bleed to
death in turn 3, because their 'perfect weenie defence' wasn't in their
first 10 cards.)

What I' ve been seeing lately is the almost total predictability of games.
If you know the decktypes, in 9 out of 10 cases you can predict what's going
to happen (barring table deals, of course.) Purely based on seating and
decktype. This is not much fun, IMO. It feels like going through the motions
for 1-2 hours. Most of what determines succes is the ability to defend
against the attacks of your predator and/ or prey, because a lot of defenses
are, for all intends and purposes, perfect. Since the game keeps on adding
new things to defend against (Events, strong ally decks and Imbued
especially), most people keep on adding more defences, because if you don't,
you can get completely screwed by seating/luck alone. And that makes the
metagame get more defensive and more defensive. Which some people like, but
I certainly don't. YMMV.

but it is very hard to pick your defense. I rarely bother against
Event defense, preferring to deal with that if I see something truly
annoying. Most of my decks will have bounce if it is a plausible add
on (only small odd dances to get dom/aus in a deck). Vote defense is
never more than a splash of cards (2-4). I don't know if I've seen
more defensive decks here, but I think I understand what you have been
seeing. People don't want to get run over in 15 minutes, so if
someone has a strong showing they are more likely to turtle up.

Maybe this is just a metagame pendulum swinging. As more defense is
stuffed in, less offense will be pack, leading to less of a need for
defense and so on. Then the deck building paradigm will shift back to
a more offense focused metagame. Defense is popular because no one
likes that helpless feeling you get when your predator steamrolls
you. And if your offense is too strong, too early then the table can
turn against you. I often play slow build up decks just to prevent
myself from a strong offense early on, finding that was a recipe for
getting assaulted by everyone.

playing at tournament level. Most likely those decks just have a big

the imbued using a host of different combat decks to know that to be
the case. Combat decks tend to be decently good at slowing down the

playing their hands, regardless of strategy. What's your point here?
Please remember that your complaint came from the amount of wins that
the Imbued have been seeing - i.e. by looking at the result - which,
by the way, is exactly when poker becomes unbalanced too.

Not that I really believe your statement about poker for a second
anyway having a rather avid poker player for a brother. One thing you
learn very quickly is that poker is never a balanced game. If I were
to play against him, for example, he would completely outclass me,
almost every time.

And, if I'm sitting with a King and Queen of Diamonds in my hand, and
there is an Ace of Diamonds, a 10 of Diamonds and a Jack of Diamonds
on the table, then regardless of what you do I will win. Isn't that an
'automatic beat'? Hence poker is unbalanced (by your definition of
balanced). Every card game must be unbalanced in order to function -
what is important, is what I have said, the power curve.

Making it reasonably balanced is the key - in other words, having some
way of justifying the position on the power curve. The imbued have
*some* severe weaknesses, especially if they manage to bump into each
other on the same table - which is just loads of laughs all round -
these weaknesses include the inability to vote, generate large amounts
of stealth or bleed, untap easily or bloat quickly. Thus I think their
resilience is pretty well-balanced against their weaknesses. It's just
a pity that combat had to be shafted again - and that's where the true
imbalance lies in my opinion. Most combat decks are just too weak to
play in tournaments, and the imbued only made matters worse for them.

off the table, although that does rely on the other players behaving
OMGOBVIOUSLY!. As far as killing cross-table vote decks, that can
